Expansion furnishing fabric

Barbara Brown’s screen-printed furnishing fabric for Heal’s: black bands that narrow, bend, and converge so that the cloth seems to bulge.

Source
V&A: Furnishing fabric “Expansion”, CIRC.269-1967
Creator
Barbara Brown (designer); Heal’s Wholesale & Export Ltd (manufacturer)
Made
1966
Style
Op art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Vibrating, high-contrast, sculptural
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.269-1967 (1165 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A catalogues the fabric with the style “Op art” and describes screen-printed cotton satin “with wide stripes in optical black-and-white undulating stripes giving the illusion of three-dimensionality”, 108 × 48 in. V&A.

The V&A’s Heal’s records say that 1960s Heal’s furnishing textiles moved from sober geometry “through Pop and Op Art-inspired motifs” to flower-power florals, under design consultant Tom Worthington. V&A.

Observed

  • Pure black on white. Three identical horizontal repeats fill the length.
  • In each repeat, vertical black bands pinch to hair-thin lines at the centre and widen into heavy wave shapes toward the edges.
  • At the top and bottom of each repeat, the bands fan out into points, so each repeat reads as a swelling drum or waist.
  • Selvedge printing along both edges gives the designer, the title, and the maker.

Why it belongs

Expansion uses the op device of progression: stripe width alone creates a curved surface on flat cloth.

It shows the style at furnishing scale, where one repeat is about the height of a person.

Borrow

Make a band narrow toward a centre line and widen toward the edges to suggest a bulge.

Repeat one large, symmetric unit vertically so that the whole panel reads as one field.
